1.pericope_label: Stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance

schools.summary: Work the vocabulary. The word rendered pure means literally separated, either by being sifted or by being held up to the light, and so unsullied, probably here untainted by sensuality; the word for mind means the faculty of moral reflection and moral understanding, and the two stand together in a passage of Plato, who used the adjective of ethical purity. Read the opening clause as evidence about the letter itself, since this already a second epistle implies no very long time since the first and much the same circle of readers; deny that the first two chapters are one letter and this the beginning of another, and set out how the last chapter answers the first. On the apostles, hold that of us is a false reading and should be your apostles, and turn this into an argument for genuineness: a true apostle, having once stated his credentials, might well sink his own personality among his colleagues from humility toward readers who owed their Christianity mainly to others, whereas a writer personating an apostle would have insisted on his assumed authority here; report the view that the forger allows the mask to slip, and call it a needless inference. Or, keeping the other reading, draw the opposite kind of conclusion, that no man would have used such language who did not regard himself and his fellow apostles as inspired and on a level with the prophets. On which commandment is meant, answer that it is surely not the whole Christian law but either the charge to beware of false teachers or, more probably, to be ready for Christ's coming; and explain why the prophets are appealed to at all, since when Peter wrote the canon of the New Testament was not complete and probably very little of it was known to these readers.

Ask first why a second letter was needed at all. Lest they should be wearied with it as though the first were sufficient, say it was not written in vain, because they needed to be often stirred up; for the minds of the godly become dim and, as it were, contract rust when admonitions cease, and even men endued with learning grow drowsy unless roused by constant warnings. Grant that they had a sincere mind, freed from the pollutions of the preceding chapter, and yet deny that their minds were on that account perfect. From this draw the use of admonition in general: the sloth of the flesh smothers the truth once received unless the goads of warning come to its aid, so that it is not enough for men to be taught what they ought to be, but there is need of godly teachers to do the second part and impress the truth deeply on the memory. On the commandment, call it a metonymy, the word standing for the doctrine taught.
Guess at the particular prophecies meant, those of Enoch mentioned by Jude, of David, and of Daniel, all founded on the same basis as the instructions of the apostles.

Find the tenderness in the manner rather than the argument, since the apostle writes the same thing in other words — it being safe for them, it should not be grievous to him — and calls them beloved, showing that ministers must be examples of love and affection as well as of life and conversation.

debates.question: Does 'the commandment of your apostles' tell for or against the letter being Peter's?

sides.position: For it: a true apostle might sink his own personality among his colleagues from humility, whereas a personator would have insisted on his assumed authority
Neither: the claim that the forger here allows the mask to slip is a needless inference
On the other reading, of us, it is the writer's own claim to inspiration — no man would speak so who did not regard himself and his fellow apostles as on a level with the prophets

debates.question: Why does the letter appeal to the prophets rather than to Christian writings?

sides.position: Because the canon of the New Testament was not complete when Peter wrote, and probably very little of it was known to these readers
Because particular prophecies were in view — those of Enoch cited by Jude, of David, and of Daniel

outliers.note: Alone turns the fact of a second letter into a doctrine of admonition, arguing that the minds of the godly contract rust when warnings cease and that teaching men what they ought to be is only half the work of a minister.
Alone traces the coherence of the whole epistle, showing that the opening of this last chapter answers the earlier charge to stir them up and its close the earlier call to make their calling sure.
Alone reads the repetition as an act of affection rather than of argument, since it was safe for them and therefore not grievous to him to write the same thing in other words.

themes: This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you; in both which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance:
That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour:

3.pericope_label: Scoffers walking after their own lusts: Where is the promise of his coming?

schools.summary: Narrow the class, since it scarcely required inspiration to foresee scoffers in general, they having abounded in every age; the apostle's eye is on a particular body of men whose reproaches would take a definite form. Insist that the phrase last days does not imply the world was about to end, and that this period might be longer than all the previous ones. On the wording, say the best authorities add in scoffing, intensifying by repetition, and note the play on words, both terms coming from a verb meaning to trifle with and neither found elsewhere. On the fathers, set out the four answers — the ancestors of the human race, the patriarchs and prophets, the first generation of Christians, and each generation in relation to the next — conclude that probably nothing more definite than our remote ancestors is meant, and refute the objection that such a scoff would be impossible in the apostle's lifetime by pointing to a passage which a writer at the close of the first century could already quote as Scripture.

Say why the warning was needed: had impious men attacked them suddenly with scoffs of this kind they might have been shaken, so he wished them to know it beforehand and be prepared to oppose such men. State the rule that follows, that the more God offers himself by the gospel to the world the more audacious will ungodly men vomit forth the poison of their impiety; and warn that nothing is more to be feared than a contest with scoffers, since it is the very extremity of evil when men treat the awful name of God with scoffs. Take the last days by the Hebrew form, the extremity of the days, and understand the days of the gospel dispensation. Then look past the wording of the scoff to what is at stake: it was a dangerous scoff, for Satan aims directly at the throat of the Church when he destroys faith in the coming of Christ, since all religion is wholly subverted unless faith in the resurrection remains firm; and state their reasoning as an argument rather than a sneer, that they set the regular course of nature in opposition to the promise of God, concluding from the world's long continuance that it would be perpetual. Alongside this, take the plainer sense of the demand, that it asks not where the promise stands written but what has become of it.

Trace the conduct to its root: the gospel requires a holy heart and holy life, and they wish to follow their own lusts, so they labour to prove it untrue in order to be rid of its injunctions, and at last persuade themselves it is a forgery. Report the addition found in almost every manuscript and version of note, that they shall come in mockery, since received into the text; and take the last days to refer probably to the conclusion of the Jewish polity, then at hand. On the scoff itself, note that they do not even deign to name him.

Expect the scoffing to increase, and explain it by the dispensation: it may seem strange that the New Testament covenant, being spiritual and therefore more agreeable to the nature of God than the Old, should be the thing ridiculed, but its spirituality and simplicity are directly contrary to the carnal mind of man, so that in the last days there will be a great improvement in the art and impudence of bantering serious godliness.

debates.question: What does 'the last days' mean here?

sides.position: The days of the gospel dispensation, by the Hebrew form 'the extremity of the days'
The last dispensation, which may itself be longer than all the previous periods — the phrase does not imply the world was about to end
Probably the conclusion of the Jewish polity, which was then at hand

debates.question: Who are 'the fathers' who fell asleep?

sides.position: Nothing more definite than our remote ancestors — and certainly not the first Christians, since the scoff is already quoted as Scripture by the close of the first century
Our first ancestors, taken plainly

outliers.note: Alone answers the critical objection at length, showing from a passage which a first-century writer could quote as Scripture that this very scoff was in existence and condemned within the apostle's lifetime.

Alone states what the scoff endangers rather than what it says, holding that Satan aims directly at the throat of the Church in destroying faith in the coming of Christ, since all religion is subverted if faith in the resurrection fails.
Alone explains why scoffing should increase precisely under the more spiritual dispensation, since the simplicity of New Testament worship is directly contrary to the carnal mind of man.

themes: Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts,
And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.

5.pericope_label: The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished

schools.summary: Put the argument as a reply to an objection: those who urged that the laws of nature were stable needed only to be shown a case in which, the same objections being available, the thing had actually happened; there was in itself as much improbability in a destruction by water as by fire, so the objection has no real force. Work on the words as well: the margin is nearer the truth with consisting for standing, the notion being coherence and order as against chaos, and out of water indicates the material the earth was made of, not that out of which it rose like an island. On the whereby, canvass the alternatives and prefer either the heavens and the earth, since both contributed to the deluge when the fountains of the great deep were broken up and the windows of heaven opened, or the water, since the apostle had the waters of the Mosaic account prominently in his eye and the antecedent of a pronoun is often what was in the writer's mind rather than the word he had used.

Answer the scoff with a single fact and make it a single argument: the world once perished by a deluge of waters, when yet it consisted of waters, and since that history was well known, those who infer the perpetuity of the world from its present state designedly close their eyes. Draw the conclusion from it: the power of nature is not sufficient to sustain the world, which contains the very element of its own ruin whenever it may please God to destroy it, for the world stands through no other power than God's word, and inferior causes derive their power from him and produce different effects as they are directed. Through water the world stood, but water could have done nothing of itself; and as soon as it pleased God to destroy the earth, the same water obeyed in becoming a ruinous inundation. So they err who stop at naked elements as though there were perpetuity in them, and the petulance of those is refuted who arm themselves with physical reasons to fight against God. Meet the objection that the world is said to have perished though the heaven was mentioned too, by answering that the heaven was then also submerged, meaning the region of the air which stood open between the two waters, the division made at the creation being then confounded. And expect the fire for the same reason as the water.

Set down the Greek and three rival translations before venturing your own, then argue the question physically: it was the opinion of the remotest antiquity that the earth was formed out of a primitive moisture, and one philosopher taught pointedly that all things derive their existence from water, which very nearly expresses the apostle's sentiment in his own terms. Support the Mosaic account from the shape of the globe, since the earth is not round but flattened at the poles and raised at the equator, the figure any soft body would assume if whirled rapidly about a centre, the equatorial diameter being greater by about twenty-five miles. Or offer a physical guess of another kind, that perhaps the interior globe of earth was fixed in the midst of the great deep, the exterior shell standing out of the water and covering it. On the present world, say it is treasured up in God's storehouse to be destroyed not by water but by fire.

debates.question: What does 'whereby' refer to — by what were the old heavens and earth destroyed?

sides.position: The heavens and the earth, since both contributed to the deluge when the fountains of the great deep were broken up and the windows of heaven opened
The water, since the apostle had the waters of the Mosaic account in his eye and the antecedent is what was in his mind rather than the word he used

debates.question: Should the physical constitution of the old world be investigated?

sides.position: Yes, and at length — from the Greek, from the opinions of antiquity, and from the oblate figure of the globe itself
Only so far as the words allow: the point is coherence and order as against chaos, and the material the earth was made of
Not at all — the fact of the deluge alone refutes the scoff, and those err who stop at naked elements as though there were perpetuity in them

outliers.note: Alone argues the Mosaic account from physical measurement, taking the flattening of the earth at the poles and the twenty-five miles of extra equatorial diameter as evidence that the globe was once a fluid mass.

Alone answers the objection that the heaven is mentioned as well as the earth, holding that the region of the air standing between the two waters was itself submerged when the division made at the creation was confounded.
Alone conjectures a structure for the antediluvian globe, with the interior fixed in the midst of the great deep and the exterior shell standing out of the water and covering it.

themes: For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water:
Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished:
But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.

8.pericope_label: One day is with the Lord as a thousand years: not willing that any should perish

schools.summary: Deny the identification with the Psalm: the first half of the saying is quite original and has no equivalent there, the second only partially parallel, so we cannot be sure the apostle had the passage in mind, though it is probable enough. Trace the saying in its other form through the second-century writers, in a martyr's dialogue, in an epistle of Barnabas, twice in one second-century father and once each in two others, noting that in no case is the context similar, and suggesting it may have been a favourite with those who held millenarian views. On the longsuffering, report the reading towards you rather than us-ward as beyond doubt, and note how natural it is that Peter should not include himself, writing mainly to Gentile Christians toward whom this longsuffering had been conspicuous.

Put the same as a discipline of the eyes: waiting seems long because we fix them on the shortness of the present life and increase our weariness by computing days and hours and minutes, whereas when the eternity of God's kingdom comes into our minds many ages vanish like so many moments. The day of resurrection depends not on the present flow of time but on the hidden purpose of God, and men wish to anticipate him because they measure time by the judgment of their own flesh and are so impatient that celerity itself is delay to them. On the longsuffering, raise the objection yourself — if God wishes none to perish, why do so many perish? — and answer by a distinction: no mention is made here of the hidden purpose of God, according to which the reprobate are doomed to their own ruin, but only of his will as made known in the gospel, where he stretches forth his hand without difference to all, but lays hold only of those whom he chose before the foundation of the world. Alongside this, narrow the promise itself, taking it first of the coming to take vengeance on the Jewish nation, delayed that the elect among them might be gathered in.

Distribute the saying over four attributes — eternity, knowledge, power and longsuffering — and read each half separately: in one day he can do the work of a thousand years, therefore he is not slow; and no delay is long to him, therefore he is longsuffering, giving us space for repentance without any inconvenience to himself. Take the saying for a quotation from the Psalm and add a pagan parallel, that a thousand or ten thousand years are but an indefinite point, or rather the smallest part of a point, compared with eternity. Then take the verse as decisive against decree: it is not slackness nor want of due displeasure at sin that makes God prolong the respite of ungodly men but his unwillingness that any should perish, and consequently he has never devised nor decreed the damnation of any man, nor made it impossible for any soul to be saved.

Say that though in the account of men there is a great difference between a day and a year, and a vast deal more between one day and a thousand years, in the account of God, who inhabits an eternity in which there is no succession, there is none, all things past and present and future being ever before him; so that the delay of a thousand years cannot be so much to him as deferring anything for an hour is to us. Make the point urgent by turning it round: if men have no belief of the eternal God they will be apt to think him such a one as themselves.

debates.question: Does the longsuffering that will have none perish rule out a decree of reprobation?

sides.position: Yes — God has never devised nor decreed the damnation of any man, nor made it impossible for any soul to be saved
No — the verse speaks only of the will made known in the gospel, where God stretches out his hand to all, not of the hidden purpose by which the reprobate are doomed to their own ruin

debates.question: Is 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years' a quotation from the Psalm?

sides.position: Yes, and the thought is a commonplace: a thousand or ten thousand years are but the smallest part of a point compared with eternity
Not certainly: the first half is quite original and has no equivalent in the Psalm, and the saying circulated independently in the second century

outliers.note: Alone follows the saying about the day and the thousand years through five second-century writers, observing that in no case is the context similar and suggesting it was a favourite with those of millenarian views.
Alone narrows the delayed promise to the coming in vengeance upon the Jewish nation, deferred so that the elect among them might be gathered in before the days of affliction were shortened.
Alone divides the saying between four attributes at once, making the first half prove that God is not slow and the second that he is longsuffering.

themes: But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

10.pericope_label: The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night

schools.summary: Reach the same possibility about the elements by a longer road: the difficulty of supposing fire destroyed by fire seems to exclude the four, and taking the two remaining ones is not satisfactory, so probably the various forms of matter are meant without specifying them; but since an early apologist calls the sun and moon and stars heavenly elements, and predictions of the last day speak of signs in them, the heavenly bodies may be intended, all the more since they follow immediately on the mention of the heavens. Pass on a commentator's ingenuity, connecting this with the word's root meaning of letters of the alphabet, for stars in the heaven are as letters on a scroll; and give the derivation from a word meaning a row, with the sense it bears in Plato. On the last clause, lay out the readings — that the works shall vanish away, shall be burned up, or shall be found, the last most strongly attested and rejected by some editors as yielding no sense — and rescue it by punctuation, placing a colon after the earth and making what follows a question, adding that happily nothing of importance turns on it; or list the same witnesses more briefly and conclude that the text seems corrupt. On the suddenness, make an argument of it: the thief, the passing away of the heavens and the reservation for fire are three reminiscences in this chapter of one discourse of Christ which only Peter and three others seem to have heard, and this may fairly be added to the evidence for the letter's authenticity.

Refuse the investigation before it starts. What follows respecting the burning of heaven and earth requires no long explanation, for it was not the apostle's purpose to speak refinedly of fire and storm, but only to introduce the exhortation he immediately adds, that we ought to strive after newness of life; and reason that as heaven and earth are to be purged by fire, the renovation of men is much more necessary. Call those interpreters mischievous who consume much labour on refined speculations when the apostle applies his doctrine to godly exhortation. Add why the warning stands here at all: we labour under two very different evils, too much haste and slothfulness, being seized with impatience for a day we at the same time securely regard as afar off, so that the sleepiness must be shaken off as well as the ardour reproved.

Do exactly what that forbids, and at length. Taking the heavens for the atmosphere in which the terrestrial vapours are lodged, set out the composition of water by weight and volume, note that passing electric sparks through the two gases produces water and passing a spark through water decomposes it again, and conclude that the noise of applying fire to so immense a quantity of aqueous particles must be terrible in the extreme; then offer a demonstration — put a drop of water on an anvil, lay red-hot iron over it and strike the iron with a hammer, and the report will be as loud as a musket. Or ask whether God has not already provided for the event and list three provisions: the stores of subterranean fire that so often burst out at burning mountains; the ethereal or electrical fire diffused through the globe, which would dissolve the frame of nature if the secret chain that binds it were loosed; and comets, one of which, returning from the sun heated two thousand times hotter than a red-hot cannon ball, would destroy all vegetables and animals long before contact. On the elements, take them for the sun, moon and stars rather than the four commonly so called, since air and water cannot melt and the earth is mentioned immediately after.

debates.question: Should the physical manner of the final conflagration be investigated?

sides.position: No — it was not the apostle's purpose to speak refinedly of fire and storm, and interpreters who spend labour on such speculations are mischievous
Yes — the chemistry of water and fire shows what the great noise must be, down to the report of a hammer struck on iron over a drop of water
Yes — and God has already provided the means, in subterranean fire, in the electrical fire diffused through the globe, and in comets

debates.question: What are the elements that shall melt?

sides.position: The sun, moon and stars, not the four commonly so called, since air and water cannot melt and the earth is named separately
Probably the various forms of matter, without specifying them — though the heavenly bodies are possible, since an early apologist calls them heavenly elements

outliers.note: Alone reduces the great noise to an experiment, arguing from a drop of water struck under red-hot iron on an anvil to the sound of the whole atmosphere's moisture meeting fire.
Alone enumerates the means already in place for the conflagration, ending with a comet which on its return from the sun would destroy all life long before it touched the earth.

Alone rescues the most strongly attested reading of the last clause by repunctuating it as a question, and alone counts the chapter's three reminiscences of one discourse of Christ as evidence for the letter's authenticity.

themes: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

11.pericope_label: What manner of persons ought ye to be, hasting unto the coming of the day of God

schools.summary: Refuse the interrogation, calling the words not a question so much as an exclamation, and say that to break the sentence there would be stiff and frigid, very unlike the fervour of this epistle. Render the plurals literally, in holy behaviours and godlinesses, noting that they indicate a variety of acts and occur here only. Prefer the margin at hasting the coming, and mean it literally: Christ's coming is hastened by holy lives, by making the gospel known to all nations so as to accomplish the number of the elect, and by praying that his kingdom come; add that the thought is singularly parallel to Peter's own speech in Solomon's Porch, and that being striking and unusual it may fairly be admitted as a note of genuineness. Or take the word of a mind anxiously desirous that the thing should occur and would accelerate it if it could, since the true Christian does not dread that day but looks to it as the period of his redemption. Draw the practical conclusion as well, that habitual contemplation of the truth that all we see is soon to pass away would make us serious, repress ambition, keep us from accumulating what must so soon be destroyed, and prompt us to lay up our treasures in heaven.

Say in one sentence that the elements of the world are to be consumed only that they may be renovated, their substance still remaining the same. Draw the moral from the plurals, that every part of the conduct should be holy and every part of godliness attended to, so that we are not to be holy in part or pious in part but to attend to every branch of duty toward man and every branch of duty toward God. And state the argument that carries it: heaven and earth shall pass away for our sakes, and their corruptions be purged by fire though as creatures of God they are pure — what then ought to be done by us, who are full of so many pollutions?

Report that some put the note of interrogation after what manner of persons ought ye to be, joining what follows to the next verse. On the dissolution, be confident that nothing is lost: all these things will be separated and decomposed but none destroyed, and being the original matter out of which the globe was formed they may enter again into a new system, which is why the apostle goes on to speak of new heavens and a new earth. Hold that the word translated hasting unto should be rendered earnestly desiring, or wishing for, which is a frequent meaning in the best Greek writers. Or use the verse to settle the extent of the destruction: all these things means the universe, the stars were made on the fourth day and will be dissolved together with the earth, and they are deceived who restrain either the history of the creation or this description of the destruction to the earth and the lower heavens, imagining the stars more ancient than the earth and likely to survive it. Close with the pagan witnesses to the same expectation, quoting a Latin poet on the time when sea and land and the palace of heaven shall burn, and reporting that the Stoics commonly held the world would catch fire when the moisture of the earth was consumed, as did the Epicureans; then notice what nobody thought, that none ever fancied it would be destroyed by water, the tradition being against it.

debates.question: Can the coming of the day of God be hastened?

sides.position: No — the word should be rendered earnestly desiring or wishing for, a frequent meaning in the best Greek writers
Yes, literally — by holy lives, by making the gospel known to all nations so as to accomplish the number of the elect, and by praying that his kingdom come
In desire only — the mind would accelerate it if it could, and welcomes it as the period of its redemption

debates.question: Does the dissolution destroy the matter of the world?

sides.position: No — all is separated and decomposed but nothing destroyed, and the same matter may enter again into a new system
No — the elements are consumed only that they may be renovated, their substance still remaining the same

outliers.note: Alone uses the verse to fix the extent of the destruction, arguing that the stars, made on the fourth day, are dissolved with the earth, against those who imagine them more ancient than the earth and likely to outlast it.
Alone assembles the pagan witnesses to a final fire, from a Latin poet and from the Stoics and Epicureans, and alone observes that no such tradition ever imagined a destruction by water.

Alone defends the unbroken sentence on grounds of style, holding that to put a question at 'ought ye to be' and make what follows the answer would be stiff and frigid, very unlike the fervour of this epistle.

themes: Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness,
Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat?

13.pericope_label: New heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness

schools.summary: Correct the emphasis of the English, which falls wrongly on we and should fall on new, and distinguish the two Greek words for new: one looks forward, young as opposed to aged, the other looks back, fresh as opposed to worn out, and it is the latter that stands here. Note that looking for is repeated three times in three verses, and read the clause about righteousness as a claim about residence — righteousness has its home there and is not a wanderer and changeful guest as on earth, from which draw the duty, that by righteousness we must make ourselves worthy of entering; certainly it is not at home in this present world, in individuals, families, or nations. On the world to come, admit at once that many of the questions naturally asked cannot easily be answered, and that whether this globe, once purified by fire, will be furnished again for the redeemed is impossible to settle with certainty; then set out three senses any of which the word would bear — a creation out of nothing once this frame is gone, which is possible though nowhere revealed; life after death upon some other of the worlds now existing, where everything would be strange, as it would be to a man carried to the planet Saturn with its wonderful ring and its seven moons; or this globe renovated and fitted up for mankind once the universal conflagration is over. Guard the order of events: sky and land are first kept in store against the day of judgment, that day then comes suddenly and the elements melt, and only afterwards are we told what to expect; nothing is said of a personal reign of Christ, nothing of saints raised to live with him below, nothing of any refurnishing before the assize — and put the weight on that silence, since this is one of the very few places where the manner of the world's closing is described.

Take the third sense without hesitation: the present globe, though destined to be burned up, will not perish but be renewed and refined, purged of every moral and natural imperfection, and made the endless dwelling of blessed spirits; and add that it is more reasonable and philosophical to conclude that it shall be refined and restored than annihilated. Insist that this condition belongs wholly after the day of judgment, on which the apostle is very express, and say plainly that it has nothing to do with what some call the millennium, since that would fall while the present order still stood.

debates.question: In what sense will the heavens and earth be new?

sides.position: Undecidable with certainty — the word would bear a creation out of nothing, life on some other existing world, or this globe renovated
This globe renovated: burned up but not destroyed, refined and purged and made the endless dwelling of blessed spirits, which is the more reasonable and philosophical conclusion

debates.question: Does this promise leave room for a millennial reign before the judgment?

sides.position: No — the order of the chapter puts the new heavens and earth after the judgment, and the total silence about a personal reign is decisive
No — the renewed state belongs wholly after the day of judgment, and has nothing to do with what some call the millennium

outliers.note: Alone illustrates the second of his three senses by supposing a man removed to the planet Saturn, with its wonderful ring and its seven moons, where every aspect of sky and dwelling-place would be new to him.
Alone distinguishes the two Greek words for new, one looking forward as young against aged and the other back as fresh against worn out, and shows that it is the latter that stands here.
Alone turns the promise into an observation about the present, that righteousness is certainly not at home in this world, whether in individuals, families, or nations.

themes: Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.

14.pericope_label: Account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation

schools.summary: Correct the construction, since found of him means rather in his sight, and note that spotless and blameless coincides with the first epistle and contrasts with the false teachers, who were called spots and blemishes; doubt that in peace has any special reference, taking it to express at once the condition and the consequence of being spotless. Weigh carefully whether the Lord here is the Father or Christ: in one verse of this chapter the Lord certainly means God, in another our Lord is expressly Jesus Christ, and the two between are disputable; but the presence of our here inclines the balance toward the latter, and had God been meant it would have sufficed to say his longsuffering — and if that is right, then throughout this weighty passage the Lord Jesus is invested with the full attributes of Deity. On the phrase our beloved brother Paul, make it a decided note of genuineness, since it implies a familiarity and equality in marked contrast to the way the sub-apostolic writers speak of him — the blessed Paul the Apostle, the sanctified and martyred, the blessed and glorious Paul, the divine Apostle — and an imitator in the second century would scarcely have attained to such freedom. Or hear both warmth and reserve in it, that Peter speaks of Paul with affection and respect yet maintains the right to criticise.

Show why the inference from hope to practice holds: hope is living and efficacious, so it cannot but attract us to itself, and he who waits for a renewed heaven must begin with renewal in himself, while they who cleave to their own filth think nothing of God's kingdom and have no taste for anything but this corrupt world. Fasten on the phrase found by him, since while the world engrosses the minds of others we must cast our eyes on the Lord, and that is real integrity which is approved by his judgment rather than that which gains the praise of men. Raise the obvious difficulty, how anyone can be found blameless when we all labour under so many deficiencies, and answer that the apostle points out the mark all the faithful are to aim at, though they cannot reach it until, having put off the flesh, they are wholly united to Christ. On the words in peace, prefer a quiet conscience founded on hope and patient waiting to peace with God, since it is because so few attend to the judgment of Christ that men are carried headlong by their lusts and are at the same time disquieted. Then, on the mention of Paul, examine all things more narrowly and conclude that it seems more probable that this epistle was composed by another according to what Peter communicated than that Peter wrote it himself, for Peter would never have spoken thus; it is enough that we have here a witness of his doctrine and goodwill who brought forward nothing contrary to what he would have said. And supply the motive for naming Paul, that unprincipled men went about to discredit him by pretending he did not agree with the other apostles, so it was necessary to take away the occasion for such a calumny.

Pass on an argument for citing Paul here at all, that the persons to whom these epistles were sent were for the most part Paul's own converts, and that he had written to several of those churches things implying that God's forbearance with sinners is intended for their salvation. Add that Paul's epistles are here ranked among the Scriptures, a term applied to those writings which are divinely inspired and to those only.

debates.question: Does the mention of Paul tell for or against Peter's authorship?

sides.position: For it — 'our beloved brother Paul' implies a familiarity and equality no second-century imitator could have attained, the sub-apostolic writers speaking of him only as blessed and glorious
For it, with reserve — Peter speaks of Paul with affection and respect yet maintains the right to criticise
Against it — on closer examination it seems more probable that the epistle was composed by another according to what Peter communicated, for Peter would never have spoken thus

debates.question: Is 'the longsuffering of our Lord' the Father's or Christ's?

sides.position: Christ's — the presence of 'our' inclines the balance, and if so the Lord Jesus is here invested with the full attributes of Deity
Christ's, taken for granted: he defers the day of his coming because he has regard for our salvation

outliers.note: Alone doubts that Peter wrote the letter, judging it more probable that another composed it from what Peter communicated, while accepting it as a faithful witness of his doctrine and goodwill.
Alone sets the phrase 'our beloved brother Paul' against the titles the sub-apostolic writers give him, and makes the difference in freedom a decided note of genuineness.
Alone remarks that Paul's epistles are here ranked among the Scriptures, a term applied to divinely inspired writings and to those only.

themes: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.
And account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you;

16.pericope_label: In which are some things hard to be understood

schools.summary: Point to the second letter to the Thessalonians, whose difficulties bristle about the very point in question, and which scoffers could turn to account by arguing that the man of sin had not yet appeared; report that many refer the words rather to justification by faith, wrested to mean faith without works, and note that Paul saw his own teaching on Christian liberty to be liable to great abuse and already abused. Say that wrest means literally to torture by the rack, and hence to strain or distort. Distinguish the unlearned here from the word so translated elsewhere, this one meaning without ordinary instruction rather than without special study, and observe that ignorance naturally produces instability, those who have no clear principles of doctrine falling easy victims to seduction. Press that the destruction is the men's own doing, emphatically so in the Greek, and that the writers of Scripture are not to blame. Then be exact against the misuse of the verse: it gives no countenance to the doctrine that all Scripture is hard and therefore not to be read by the people, since all that is said is that some Scripture is hard and that bad men make a bad use of the fact; and the inference drawn is not do not read, nor even pass over what seems hard, but be on your guard against interpretations contrary to the spirit of the gospel. On the other scriptures, hold that the Old Testament can hardly be meant and that Christian writings of some kind are intended, perhaps including some that are not canonical.

Settle on Hebrews as the particular epistle referred to, on the ground that the subjects in view are those of the preceding verses — the day of judgment, the future state and the need to be ready for it — and that the promise of a renewed heaven and earth answers exactly to the better and heavenly country of that epistle, whose warnings coincide with the exhortation given here. Then state the principle about reading: we are not forbidden to read Paul's epistles because they contain things hard to be understood, but rather they are commended to us, provided we bring a calm and teachable mind; the apostle condemns men who are trifling and volatile, and though the same is commonly done to all Scripture, he does not conclude that we are not to read it, but that the vices which prevent improvement ought to be corrected. Allow the obscurity and explain it, that it is nothing to wonder at in the mysteries of Christ's kingdom, since many are blind who stumble at midday.

Set out the alternative readings: with the common one the hard things are the matters spoken of, but on the reading of several manuscripts and versions the difficulties are in all the epistles — and indeed, in what ancient writings are there not difficulties? Give the force of the verb, to distort, to put to the rack, to overstretch and dislocate the limbs, and say the persons meant are those who proceed by no fair plan of interpretation but force unnatural and sophistical meanings on the word of God. Then argue at length against withholding the Scriptures from the common people, and close with a challenge, that a single instance cannot be adduced of any soul perverted or destroyed by reading the Bible, and that the insinuation is blasphemous. Or say it in one line: that some use the Scriptures ill is no reason why others should not use them at all. And take the phrase the other scriptures to prove that Paul's writings were by then part of Scripture.

debates.question: Which of Paul's letters is referred to?

sides.position: Hebrews — its better and heavenly country answers exactly to the new heavens and new earth, and its warnings coincide with the exhortation here
The second letter to the Thessalonians, whose difficulties bristle about the very point in question, the time of Christ's coming
All of them, on the manuscript reading which makes the difficulties lie in the epistles rather than in the things spoken of

debates.question: What are 'the other scriptures' that are also wrested?

sides.position: Christian writings of some kind, perhaps including uncanonical ones — the Old Testament can hardly be meant without some intimation of so novel a grouping
Scripture at large — and the phrase proves that Paul's writings were by then reckoned part of it

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a sustained argument against withholding the Bible from the laity, closing with the challenge that no single instance can be produced of a soul destroyed by reading it.

Alone states precisely what the verse does and does not concede, that some Scripture is hard rather than all, and that the inference drawn is not to stop reading but to guard against interpretations contrary to the spirit of the gospel.
Alone accounts for the obscurity itself, holding it no wonder in the mysteries of Christ's kingdom, since many are blind who stumble at midday while others rush through devious paths into ruin.

themes: As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.

17.pericope_label: Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour

schools.summary: Notice where the word for being carried away is used elsewhere and find it strange: of its three places in the New Testament, one is the account of Barnabas being carried away with the dissimulation of Peter himself. Observe that the word for steadfastness occurs nowhere else, and that this verse and the last both refer back to the opening, so that the coherence between beginning and ending is complete. From the absence of any directions as to how these evil men and their victims are to be treated, which the epistle of Jude gives rather elaborately, argue that this letter is the earlier, since when evil men begin to arise the first impulse is to avoid them, whereas when they have established themselves people begin to consider how to deal with the seducers and win back the seduced. Argue the same way from the ending, which is abrupt and has no greetings: this is so unlike the first epistle and apostolic letters generally that so accomplished an imitator would scarcely have omitted them, doubly natural as they would be in one personating an apostle near the end of his life; assume the apostle himself is writing, and the disappointment is explained, his heart being too full of the dangers threatening the whole community to think of himself. On the doxology, say there can be no doubt that here homage is paid to Jesus Christ as true God, and suggest this may be the earliest example of that hymn to Christ as God which a Roman governor reported to his emperor that the Christians sang before daybreak. Add the sterner point that, being forewarned, they are without excuse for misunderstanding either Peter or Paul.

Meet the difficulty the warning raises. It seems that we stand on slippery ground and that the certainty of our salvation hangs as it were on a thread, since the faithful are told to take heed lest they fall from their own steadfastness; what then will become of us if we are exposed to the danger of falling? Answer that such exhortations are by no means intended to shake the firmness of that faith which rests on God, but to correct the sloth of our flesh: as long as we are in the flesh our tardiness must be roused, and it is fitly roused by having our weakness and the dangers around us set before our eyes, without the confidence which rests on God's promises being shaken. On growth, say it is the only way of persevering, to make continual advances and not stand still in the middle of the journey. And on the doxology, call it a remarkable passage to prove the divinity of Christ, since what is said cannot belong to any but God alone, noting that the word now is designed so that we may not rob Christ of his glory during our warfare here.

Argue growth from the body. The life of a Christian is a growth, since he is at first born of God and a little child, becomes a young man and a father in Christ, and every father was once an infant; in the order of nature the infant that does not grow daily is sickly and soon dies, and so in grace; many boast of their conversion who were never more than babes and have long since lost even that. Or say there may be for a time grace without growth, as there may be natural life without growth, but such sickly life will end in death and every day draw nigher to it; the strength of a Christian depends on what his soul feeds on, and sin of every kind starves it. On the close, take the day of eternity for that in which death and misery and trial and time itself are at an end, a day without night, without interruption, without end.

debates.question: If the faithful can fall from their steadfastness, how is salvation certain?

sides.position: Such warnings are not meant to shake the faith that rests on God but to correct the sloth of the flesh, which must be roused as long as we are in the flesh
The warning is simply a duty of vigilance: being forewarned by prophets and apostles, they are without excuse if they are led away

debates.question: Does the abrupt, greetingless ending tell for or against the letter being Peter's?

sides.position: For it: so accomplished an imitator would scarcely have omitted greetings, which would be doubly natural in one personating an apostle near the end of his life
It is simply the overflow of the whole chapter's feeling, ending in a tribute of praise

outliers.note: Alone argues the priority of this epistle to Jude from what is missing in it, since directions for dealing with seducers and reclaiming their victims belong to a later stage than the first impulse to avoid them.
Alone presses the analogy of infancy against resting in conversion, observing that many who boast of the grace they received were never more than babes and have long since lost even that.

Alone raises the objection that the warning appears to hang salvation on a thread, and answers that exhortations of this kind correct the sloth of the flesh without shaking the confidence that rests on God's promises.

themes: Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.
But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
